t: Maximum of Minimum Values in All Subarrays -- Spans of Minimums
o: For every window size w from 1 to n we need the largest window-minimum. Example [0,1,2,4] resolves to [4,2,1,0]: alone, 4 is the biggest single-element minimum; pairs peak at min(2,4) = 2; triples peak at min(1,2,4) = 1; the whole array bottoms out at 0. Answers only shrink as windows grow. The pivotal observation: nums[k] is the minimum of every window containing k that fits between the nearest smaller elements on each side. With n up to 10^5, recomputing minimums per size is too slow, so we invert the question -- for which window sizes does each element serve as the winning maximum-of-minimums?
k: nums[k] is the minimum of exactly the windows lying inside (left[k], right[k]) where those bounds are the nearest smaller neighbors; the count right[k] - left[k] - 1 of window sizes it wins is called its span.
ans[w-1] equals the maximum value among elements whose span is at least w -- computable by bucketing values per span and taking a suffix maximum.
Monotonic stacks find nearest-smaller boundaries for all positions in O(n); popping with >= on one side and > on the other distributes tied minimums consistently.

a.n: Approach 1: Rolling Window Minimums Per Size
a.i: Keep the minimums of all windows of the current size, then derive the next size by pairing each entry with the element entering on the right: winPrime[i] = min(win[i], nums[i+w]). Recording the maximum after every step answers queries in order using a single rolling buffer.
s: Start with win = nums, the minimums of all size-1 windows.
Shrink: winPrime[i] = min(win[i], nums[i + currentSize]) for each surviving start.
Repeat until the window covers the entire array.
a.t: O(n^2) -- window sizes contribute lengths n, n-1, ..., 1 of work in total
a.sp: O(n) -- one rolling buffer of current window minimums

a.n: Approach 2: Monotonic Stack Spans Plus Suffix Maximum
a.i: Compute each element span with two stack passes: previous strictly-smaller index and next smaller-or-equal index (the asymmetry hands tied minimums to exactly one owner). Bucket every value under its span, then sweep spans from large to small carrying a running maximum so best[w] ends holding the best value available for every window size <= w.
s: Stack pass left to right recording each position previous strictly smaller index.
Stack pass right to left recording each position next smaller-or-equal index.
Set best[span] = max(best[span], nums[i]) with span = right - left - 1.
a.t: O(n) -- two amortized-linear stack passes plus linear bucketing
a.sp: O(n) -- boundary arrays, the stack, and the span buckets

w: Lead with the brute-force rolling minimum to establish the non-increasing answer shape, then deliver the span argument -- it is the interview-winning insight and the same trick behind largest rectangle in a histogram. Pitfalls: tie handling (strict on one side, non-strict on the other), or equal minimums get double-counted and inflate answers; the suffix-max step is mandatory because an element with a large span also wins smaller windows. Edge cases: n = 1 returns the element itself, and duplicates like [10,20,50,10] exercise the tie logic. Follow-ups: answering one arbitrary w via binary search over the answer with a sliding-window minimum, or a streaming variant.
